bill_analysis: Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025 Overview The Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025, seeks to facilitate earlier legislative consideration of certain treaty commitments and strengthen the flow of information between the Executive and the Legislature regarding Nigeria’s international obligations. The Bill proposes amendments to the Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act, Cap. T20, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004 (the principal Act), by requiring specified categories of treaties to be transmitted to the National Assembly within 90 days of negotiation and before ratification. The requirement applies to treaties falling within Section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the Act, namely: a) law-making treaties, being agreements constituting rules governing inter-state relations and cooperation in any area of endeavour which alter or modify existing legislation or affect the legislative powers of the National Assembly, and b) agreements that impose financial, political, or social obligations on Nigeria, or that are of scientific or technological import. The Bill also inserts a new subsection (3) into Section 4 of the principal Act, requiring the Attorney-General of the Federation to notify the National Assembly quarterly on the status of ratified treaties in Nigeria. The proposed amendments respond to longstanding concerns regarding the implementation and domestication of treaties within Nigeria’s legal system. Although Nigeria is party to a substantial number of treaties, conventions, and related international instruments, many have not been domesticated through legislation and therefore do not have the force of law within Nigeria despite creating binding international obligations. The Bill seeks to ensure that the National Assembly is informed of specified categories of treaties before ratification and receives periodic updates on ratified agreements. In doing so, it aims to support earlier legislative consideration of treaty commitments and strengthen institutional engagement with Nigeria’s international obligations. Constitutional and Statutory Framework for Treaty-Making The constitutional framework for treaty implementation is established by Section 12 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), which provides that no treaty shall have the force of law in Nigeria unless it has been enacted by the National Assembly. Nigeria, therefore, operates a dualist system in which the ratification of a treaty at the international level does not, without more, make its provisions enforceable. Under this arrangement, the Executive negotiates and ratifies treaties on behalf of Nigeria, while the National Assembly determines whether those treaties should be incorporated into domestic law through legislation. Section 12 further empowers the National Assembly to enact laws for the implementation of treaties. However, if a law intended to implement a treaty deals with matters outside the Exclusive Legislative List, it must first be approved by a majority of the State Houses of Assembly before the President can assent to it. The Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act supplements this constitutional framework by distinguishing between different categories of treaties and prescribing procedures applicable to them. Section 3(1) classifies treaties into three categories: a) treaties that alter or modify existing laws or affect legislative powers b) treaties that impose financial, political, social, scientific, or technological obligations c) treaties relating to cultural and educational exchange. While the Act classifies treaties for procedural purposes, it does not establish a comprehensive statutory framework governing treaty negotiation, consultation, legislative engagement, implementation, or post-ratification monitoring. Previous Reform Efforts Efforts to reform Nigeria’s treaty-making framework have been ongoing for several years. A recurring concern has been the limited involvement of the National Assembly during the early stages of treaty development. Legislative engagement often occurs only when domestication becomes necessary, by which time Nigeria may already have assumed binding international obligations. In 2016, two separate Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act (Amendment) Bills proposed earlier engagement with the National Assembly. The Bills required consultation with the appropriate committees before treaties were signed and proposed that treaties be transmitted to relevant committees within 90 days of signature. In 2020, the Treaties (Making Procedure) Act (Repeal and Re-enactment) Bill proposed more extensive reforms. It required approval by both Houses of the National Assembly before treaties could be signed and further required that treaties be transmitted to the National Assembly and the Federal Ministry of Justice within one month of signature. Although these Bills did not become law, they reflect a consistent concern that treaty information often reaches the National Assembly too late in the process to facilitate meaningful legislative engagement or support timely domestication. The current Bill continues this reform trajectory by seeking to provide earlier access to information concerning specified treaty commitments. Assessment of the Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025 The Bill represents a measured effort to strengthen legislative engagement within Nigeria’s treaty framework by requiring the transmission of specified categories of treaties to the National Assembly before ratification. Earlier access to treaty information may assist legislators in identifying potential legal, financial, and policy implications before Nigeria assumes binding international obligations. The requirement for quarterly notification on ratified treaties also introduces a structured mechanism for communication between the Executive and the Legislature regarding treaty commitments. The Bill preserves the constitutional allocation of responsibilities between the Executive and the Legislature. It does not alter the Executive’s role in negotiating and ratifying treaties, nor does it modify the constitutional requirement that treaties must be enacted by the National Assembly before acquiring the force of law in Nigeria. Rather, it seeks to improve the flow of treaty-related information within the existing constitutional framework. Certain aspects of the Bill may nevertheless benefit from further consideration. 1. Absence of Consequences for Non-Compliance The Bill requires the transmission of specified treaties to the National Assembly within 90 days of negotiation, but does not specify the consequences of a failure to comply with that requirement. The absence of an enforcement mechanism may raise questions regarding how the obligation will operate in practice and the extent to which compliance can be ensured. 2. Scope of Excluded Treaties The Bill applies only to treaties falling within Section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the principal Act and does not extend to cultural and educational exchange agreements under Section 3(1)(c). While this approach follows the existing statutory classification of treaties, some agreements within the excluded category may have financial, institutional, or policy implications that could warrant legislative consideration before ratification. 3. Reporting on Ratified Treaties The requirement for quarterly notification by the Attorney-General introduces a mechanism through which the National Assembly may receive regular information concerning treaty commitments. The usefulness of this reporting process may be enhanced through guidance on the categories of information to be included in such notifications, particularly where the objective is to support legislative engagement with domestication and implementation efforts. 4. Scope of the Existing Statutory Framework The current framework leaves some uncertainty regarding the extent to which the Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act applies to treaties relating to matters outside the Exclusive Legislative List. This issue arises from the relationship between Section 12(2) of the 1999 Constitution, which empowers the National Assembly to make laws for the implementation of treaties on matters not included in the Exclusive Legislative List, and Section 1(1) of the Act, which applies the treaty-making procedures under the Act to treaties on matters contained in the Exclusive Legislative List. Recommendations 1. Clarify Compliance with the Transmission Requirement The Bill should clarify the consequences of failing to transmit treaties to the National Assembly within the prescribed period. Greater certainty regarding the effect of non-compliance would strengthen accountability and support consistent implementation of the proposed requirement. 2. Review the Scope of Treaties Covered by the Bill The exclusion of cultural and educational exchange agreements under Section 3(1)(c) of the principal Act may warrant further examination. Some agreements within this category may create substantial financial, institutional, or policy commitments that could benefit from legislative consideration before ratification. 3. Provide Greater Detail on Reporting Requirements The reporting obligation imposed on the Attorney-General could be strengthened by identifying the information to be included in quarterly notifications. Information relating to domestication, implementation measures, responsible institutions, and the status of treaty obligations would assist the National Assembly in monitoring treaty commitments and their domestic effect. 4. Consider Comprehensive Reform of the Treaty-Making Act The Bill addresses the transmission of treaty information and reporting on ratified treaties but does not deal with other aspects of treaty governance. Future reform efforts may provide an opportunity to examine whether the Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act should establish a more comprehensive framework governing treaty negotiation, consultation, implementation, monitoring, and domestication. Conclusion The Treaty (Making Procedure, etc.) Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025, introduces targeted reforms aimed at strengthening engagement between the Executive and the Legislature within Nigeria’s treaty framework. By requiring the transmission of specified treaties to the National Assembly before ratification and mandating periodic notification by the Attorney-General regarding the status of ratified treaties, the Bill seeks to facilitate earlier legislative consideration of treaty commitments. The Bill preserves the existing constitutional allocation of responsibilities in treaty-making while creating additional mechanisms through which treaty-related information may be shared with the National Assembly. It responds to longstanding concerns regarding treaty domestication and legislative engagement without altering the constitutional structure governing the negotiation, ratification, and implementation of treaties. The Bill therefore represents an incremental reform directed at improving oversight and information-sharing within the existing framework. Its effectiveness will depend on the consistency of implementation and the extent to which the information provided through transmission and reporting mechanisms supports legislative consideration of treaty obligations and their domestic implementation.
